content.title: Who is Braylon Mullins, UConn's March Madness hero who sank Duke with his epic logo shot?
content.text: The hero of one of the greatest games in NCAA tournament history initially wanted no part of attempting the winning shot.When he retrieved Duke freshman Cayden Boozer’s deflected pass near mid-court, UConn’s Braylon Mullins wasted no time whipping a pass to teammate Alex Karaban on the right wing. Mullins, after all, was mired in a month-long shooting slump from behind the arc and had missed all four 3-pointers he had previously tried on Sunday night.Advertisement“I looked at the clock and it said five seconds,” Mullins told CBS sideline reporter Tracy Wolfson, “so I tried to get the ball to someone who had made one in the game.”That would have been the end of Mullins’ involvement in the play, except that Karaban did not have space to get off a shot and passed it right back to the UConn freshman with less than three seconds to go in regulation. That left Mullins with little choice but to rise and fire from the edge of the mid-court logo.What happened next will be replayed for decades in March Madness highlight montages. Mullins buried a last-second 35-footer to secure a 73-72 victory, sending second-seeded UConn to the Final Four for the third time in four years and ending Duke’s season in the most heartbreaking possible way.Duke, the NCAA tournament’s No. 1 overall seed, led by 19 late in the first half, by 10 with less than seven minutes to go and by two with possession of the ball in the final 10 seconds. Somehow, someway, the Blue Devils lost, becoming the first No. 1 seed to lose when leading by 15 or more points at halftime in the NCAA tournament in 135 tries.Advertisement“When I saw Braylon, for some reason I had the gut instinct to pass it to him,” Karaban said. “I looked at the rim and there was five seconds left, and I thought maybe something better could develop. I had Cam Boozer in front of me, which was a harder, more difficult shot, so I passed it to Braylon. When I saw him release it, I was like, that really might go in.”Mullins’ game-winner is the deepest game-winning shot ever hit in the final seconds of an NCAA tournament game by a team trailing by two points. Only 2005 Louisville has ever rallied from a deficit larger than 19 points to win an Elite Eight game.In a way, it wasn’t just Duke that Mullins sent home with his impossibly deep 3-pointer. As a native of Greenfield, Indiana, Mullins will also be returning home when UConn faces Illinois in the national semifinals in Indianapolis next Saturday.AdvertisementMullins is the son of Josh Mullins, an athletic 6-foot-6 guard who played for Lincoln Trail College and for IUPUI from 1999-2003. He averaged 12.2 points for the IUPUI team that became the school’s first to make the NCAA tournament in 2003, but the Jaguars lost 95-64 to Kentucky in the first round that year.UConn's Braylon Mullins (24) validated his coach, Dan Hurley, who chose to trust the freshman in the closing seconds of their Elite Eight win over Duke. (Scott Taetsch/NCAA Photos via Getty Images) (Scott Taetsch via Getty Images)Josh Mullins went into coaching when he became a father and raised a son who went on to achieve more in basketball than he ever did. At Greenfield-Central High School, Braylon initially was known as a sharpshooter who opponents couldn’t afford to leave open in the corner. Then, as time went on, he blossomed into something more.Braylon Mullins became a five-star recruit, a McDonald’s All-American and Indiana’s 2025 Mr. Basketball. As a senior in high school, he averaged 32.9 points, 7.2 rebounds, 4.2 assists and 3.7 steals while leading Greenfield-Central to a 23-4 record.AdvertisementThe summer before his senior year of high school, Mullins had his choice of virtually any college in the country, including Duke. Mullins chose UConn over fellow finalists Indiana and North Carolina because of the relationship he built with Huskies coach Dan Hurley.‘He’s a critical threat on offense’It hasn’t been the smoothest freshman season for Mullins, but the 6-foot-6 shooting guard has showcased elite shooting mechanics, high basketball IQ, the ability to move off ball and a knack for defending his position. He’s averaging 12.0 points per game this season despite shooting only 33.5 % from behind the arc.“I think what a lot of people miss with Braylon is just how well he's able to hold up for us defensively and how well he's able to hold up for us on the backboard from a physicality standpoint,” UConn coach Dan Hurley told reporters earlier this NCAA tournament. “You don't get far in this tournament unless your freshmen can do that. Like the guy, he's a three-way player. He's out on the glass. He's a critical threat on offense, but he's also like an underrated defensive player with a maturity about him where, if he goes through stretches of the game where he's not getting shots, not making shots, he keeps playing winning basketball.”AdvertisementThat’s exactly why Mullins was on the floor down the stretch on Sunday despite going 0-for-4 from behind the arc up to that point. Hurley wanted his most disruptive defensive players to try to make a play with Duke inbounding the ball up two in the waning seconds.Hurley again showed his trust in Mullins after guard Solo Ball deflected Cayden Boozer’s pass. The UConn coach chose not to call timeout when Mullins retrieved the loose ball and he and Karaban passed the ball back and forth.“It's scary, man,” Hurley said. "It's instincts. It's gut instinct. But I think with their size, their length, their ability to switch everything, it just felt like the window where you've just got to let March Madness take over, March Magic.”AdvertisementMarch Magic smiled on UConn.The kid who was 10-for-57 from 3-point range over his past nine games picked the best possible time to regain his shooting stroke.
